outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of the text:

I plan to be the world's foremost authority on peafowl. I believe I'll be offered a chair someday at the chicken college. —Flannery O'Connor

It's certainly kind of you to want to give me that dog. However, I raise peacocks, and one cannot keep dogs and peafowl on the same property. Visitors here must leave their dogs in the car, or else the peachicks take to the trees in fits of nervous prostration. I currently have twenty-seven of them, and the place sounds like a jungle at night—they yell and scream at the slightest atmospheric disturbance or mechanical noise.

Sitting on the back steps, I spend my days contemplating how they might best decorate the lawn. They much prefer perching on the tractors, atop the chicken house, or on a garbage can lid. I've simply adjusted to their tastes, which happen to be decidedly anti-dog.

So thank you, but I'll take the thought in place of the dog itself. I do appreciate your wanting to give it to me. Do come visit, though—there's nothing to do here but sit, walk, collect chigger bites, and let me show you a peacock before his tail grows ragged.
outputs.L2:
I intend to become the foremost expert on peafowl in the world. I expect some chicken college will eventually offer me a professorship. —Flannery O'Connor

It's very kind of you to offer me that dog, but I have to decline. Since I keep peacocks, dogs simply don't mix with them on my property. Visitors here have learned to leave their pets locked in the car—otherwise the peachickens panic and flee into the trees, practically having nervous breakdowns. Currently I have twenty-seven of them, and after dark this place sounds absolutely like a jungle. The smallest disturbance in the air or the faintest mechanical racket sets them screeching and hollering.

I often sit on the back porch for hours, contemplating how these birds might best be arranged for visual effect on the property. Instead of the lawn, though, they prefer perching on tractors, atop the chicken coop, or on garbage can lids. I've simply learned to accommodate their preferences, which happen to be firmly anti-canine.

So thank you, but I'll accept the gesture rather than the actual dog—I do appreciate the generous offer. Do stop by sometime, though. There's not much to occupy you here besides sitting around, taking a stroll, getting chigger bites, and admiring a peacock while his tail feathers are still in good shape.

# On Peafowl, Dogs, and the Simple Pleasures of Home

Flannery O'Connor, with her characteristic wit and self-deprecating humor, once declared her growing ambition to become nothing less than the world's foremost authority on peafowl. She joked that at this rate of dedicated study and accumulation of birds, she fully expected to be offered an honorary chair at some "chicken college"—a wry acknowledgment of how her modest hobby had blossomed into something approaching scholarly obsession.

This obsession, however, came with practical complications, chief among them the fundamental incompatibility between her peacocks and any visiting canines. She explained, with the patient tone of someone who has had to give this explanation many times before, that peacocks and dogs simply cannot coexist peacefully on her property. Any visitor hoping to call on her would need to leave their dog safely in the car, lest the mere presence of the animal send her peachickens fleeing in panic up into the trees, undoing weeks of careful acclimation and no small amount of her patience.

By this point in her peafowl-keeping career, O'Connor had amassed a flock of twenty-seven birds, and she delighted in describing the cacophony they produced. At the slightest disturbance—a car door, an unfamiliar footstep, even a shift in the wind—the birds would erupt into their distinctive, piercing calls, transforming her quiet rural home into something that sounded, especially after dark, like a jungle alive with exotic and unseen creatures. It was, she implied, both an inconvenience and a source of considerable pride.

She went on to describe the birds' idiosyncratic habits with evident affection, noting their peculiar fondness for perching in the most unlikely places: atop tractors left out in the yard, on the roofs of chicken houses, or balanced precariously on garbage can lids. These preferences, odd as they were, had to be accommodated alongside the birds' unwavering aversion to dogs, and O'Connor had long since arranged her household and her expectations of visitors around this immutable fact of peacock nature.

Ultimately, she gently but firmly declined an offer to accept a dog as a gift, all while extending a warm invitation for the person to come visit her instead. She promised that such a visit would offer its own simple but genuine pleasures—not least among them the chance to see one of her peacocks in full display before the season inevitably arrived when the magnificent tail feathers would molt and lose their splendor, leaving the bird, until the following year, a rather more ordinary-looking creature.

# On Declining a Dog

Dear Margaret,

I want to thank you for thinking of me, and for the generous offer of the puppy from your neighbor's litter. I know you meant it kindly, and I know that most people would be delighted at the prospect of a good farm dog. But I'm afraid I have to decline, and I want to explain why, because I don't think it's obvious unless you've spent as much time as I have watching peafowl go about their business.

I have twenty-seven peacocks and peahens now—the number crept up on me, as these things do—and if there is one thing I have learned about them, it is that they are not birds who adapt easily to change. They are creatures of fixed habit and considerable nervousness, and a dog, however well-behaved, represents exactly the kind of disruption they cannot tolerate.

You have to understand how they spend their days. My peacocks are forever perching on the tractor in the side yard, arranging themselves along the hood and the fender as though it were built for that purpose. They favor the roof of the chicken house too, where they can survey the whole property like small feathered sentries. These are not casual choices. Once a peacock decides that the tractor is his post, he returns to it day after day, and woe to anything that tries to occupy that space or even wander too near it.

And they are loud about their displeasure. Anyone who has never lived with peafowl cannot imagine the sound they make when something upsets them—a scream that carries clear across the fields and rattles the windows. I have heard it triggered by nothing more than a shifted feed bucket or an unfamiliar car in the drive. A dog, trotting about the yard with a dog's natural curiosity, sniffing at the tractor tires or investigating the chicken house, would set them off constantly. The peacocks would scream, the peahens would scatter, and the whole delicate order of the place would collapse into chaos.

I have watched them grow skittish over far less. A strange cat passing through will send half the flock into an uproar that takes hours to settle. I can only imagine what a dog—an animal peafowl seem to regard as a natural enemy, whether or not it means them any harm—would do to their nerves, and mine along with them.

So you see, it isn't that I dislike dogs, or that I don't appreciate your thoughtfulness. It's simply that I have already chosen my companions, twenty-seven of them, each with opinions and habits as fixed as any I've ever encountered in a person, and I have learned that keeping peace among them means arranging my whole life around their particular ways. A dog does not fit into that arrangement, no matter how sweet-tempered he might be.

Give the puppy my regards, and find him a home where he can chase things to his heart's content without causing a feathered catastrophe. As for me, I'll be out by the tractor, no doubt, coaxing some indignant peacock down off the hood before he decides to make a scene.

With affection and no small amount of peacock-induced exhaustion,

Eleanor

# On Belief and the Grotesque: Flannery O'Connor's Sacramental Vision

Flannery O'Connor occupies a singular place in American literature, not merely as a stylist of the Southern Gothic but as a writer whose entire body of work was animated by a fierce and uncompromising belief. To read O'Connor without understanding the depth of her Catholic faith is to miss the very engine driving her fiction—the violent grace, the grotesque characters, the moments of shattering revelation that punctuate stories like "A Good Man Is Hard to Find" and novels like *Wise Blood*.

O'Connor believed that fiction should not merely reflect the world but should pierce through its surface to reveal deeper spiritual realities, however uncomfortable or disturbing. She once wrote that to the hard of hearing you shout, and for the almost blind you draw large and startling figures. This was her artistic credo: in an increasingly secular age, she believed the writer of faith had to use shock, violence, and the grotesque to make readers see what they had grown numb to—the presence of grace operating in a fallen world.

Her characters are frequently unlikeable, even repugnant—self-satisfied intellectuals, bigots, con men, and murderers. Yet O'Connor's belief in redemption meant that even her most flawed characters were candidates for grace, often delivered through violent or absurd circumstances. The Misfit's chilling proclamation in "A Good Man Is Hard to Find," or Hazel Motes's self-blinding in *Wise Blood*, are not gratuitous cruelties but manifestations of her conviction that suffering and confrontation with mortality can crack open the hardest hearts.

Critics have sometimes struggled with the disjunction between O'Connor's devout belief and the seeming bleakness of her narratives. But for O'Connor, this was no contradiction. She believed the grotesque was simply what the sacred looked like when glimpsed by an audience that had lost the language of faith. Her stories don't offer comfort in the conventional sense; they offer confrontation—with sin, with mystery, with the possibility that grace might arrive in forms almost too strange or terrible to recognize.

Flannery O'Connor died young, at thirty-nine, after a long battle with lupus, yet she left behind a body of work whose theological seriousness and literary craft continue to challenge and unsettle readers. Her belief was not decorative but structural—it shaped every plot twist, every grotesque image, every moment where a character is stripped of pretense and left, quite literally, staring into the abyss or into the face of God. In this way, O'Connor's fiction remains a testament to the idea that literature can be both an act of belief and an instrument of unsettling truth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short first-person letter in the voice of Flannery O'Connor politely declining a gift of a dog because she raises peacocks, using her dry wit and Southern rural detail.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Mrs. Fitzgerald,

Thank you kindly for the offer of the spaniel pup. It was good of you to think of me, and I don't doubt he's a fine specimen, all ears and apology the way spaniels are. But I'll have to decline him, and I hope you won't hold it against me or think me ungracious, because the fault lies entirely with the peafowl.

I have forty-some peacocks here at Andalusia now, and they have made it clear, in their opinion, that the place is theirs and I am merely the woman who fills the feed pans. They do not care for dogs. They do not care for much of anything, being vain, screaming, magnificent creatures put on this earth, I am convinced, to remind us that God has a sense of humor and no small taste for the gaudy. A dog underfoot would only give them one more thing to despise, and a peacock with a grievance is a peacock who will let you know it at five o'clock in the morning, every morning, until Judgment Day.

I have tried to explain to them that a spaniel is a gentle animal, not a threat to anyone's tail feathers, but you cannot reason with a peacock any more than you can reason with a Bible salesman or a case of lupus, and I have some experience with all three. Better not to try. Better to let them have their dominion in peace and me have mine, such as it is, on the porch with the aluminum crutches and the typewriter.

So the pup will have to find some other household to grace, one unburdened by fowl of such operatic temperament. I have no doubt he'll land well—he has the look of a dog who lands well.

With gratitude all the same, and my best to Robert,

Flannery
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a humorous fictional letter where a peacock-obsessed farmwoman explains why she can't accept a dog as a gift, mimicking Flannery O'Connor's tone and style.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Mrs. Turpin,

I received your letter of the 14th, along with the photograph of the dog, and I want to thank you for your generosity even though I cannot accept what you are offering. I know you meant well. People always mean well when they try to give you a dog, the way they mean well when they tell you that you ought to see a doctor about that look you've been wearing lately. I have looked at the picture a good long while, turning it in the light, and I will say the animal has an honest face, for a dog. But an honest face is not enough to recommend an creature to this household, not with what I am already keeping out back.

You will understand, I think, once I explain the situation with the peacocks.

I have eleven of them now, thirteen if you count the two that only show up around suppertime like poor relations, and I have come to believe that the Lord, in His inscrutable wisdom, did not intend for peacocks and dogs to occupy the same fifty acres of Georgia clay. It is not that the peacocks are jealous, exactly, though I have caught the old cock giving the mailman a look that would curdle fresh milk, and the mailman is not a dog. It is more that a dog and a peacock cannot agree on what the yard is for. A dog thinks the yard is for barking at trucks and burying things it will forget about by Tuesday. A peacock knows the yard is a theater, and he is not going to share the stage with an animal whose idea of art is rolling in something dead.

I have watched my peacocks stand for the better part of an hour with their tails up, catching the light just so, as if they were under the impression that God Himself might be watching from behind a cloud, and taking notes. There is something almost holy in it, though I would not say that to the preacher, who already thinks I have my priorities backward on account of the chicken coop being nicer than the church annex. A dog does not stand still long enough to be holy. A dog is all appetite and apology, which I understand is the condition of most of mankind, but I did not put up a fence to keep mankind out only to invite its four-legged version in through the front gate.

There is also the matter of Brother, my oldest peacock, who has never in his life backed down from anything smaller than a pickup truck, and who would regard a dog as either a rival for the yard or a slow-moving hors d'oeuvre, I have not decided which, and I would rather not find out at the cost of your nephew's dog's tail feathers, so to speak, though I understand dogs do not have tail feathers, which is really the whole of my objection stated plainly. A peacock has a hundred eyes in his tail, put there, I believe, so that Something is always watching, even when the rest of us have gotten careless. A dog has two eyes, both usually fixed on whatever you are eating, and no capacity whatsoever for symbolism.

I do not say this to be unkind about the dog, who I am sure is a fine animal and will make somebody a good companion, somebody whose yard is not already a congregation of blue-green prophets. I only say that a woman can keep the peacocks or she can keep her peace, and I have chosen, God help me, the peacocks.

Give the dog to the Fitzgeralds. They have a flat, uninteresting yard that could use the company.

Yours in Christ and feathers,
Ruby Ansley
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine you are Flannery O'Connor writing to a friend who offered her a puppy—craft a witty refusal that includes details about her peacocks' behavior and quirks.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear ————,

I thank you kindly for the offer of the puppy, but I must decline, and I want you to understand it is nothing personal against the puppy, who I am sure is a fine specimen of ignorant devotion. The trouble is I already have forty-odd fools strutting around this place who require my constant attention and give me next to nothing in return except the occasional heart attack when they scream bloody murder at three in the morning for no reason I have ever been able to determine. I refer, of course, to the peacocks.

You would think a dog would be a restful change from these birds, but I have got to the point where I can't imagine sharing the yard with a creature that displays affection or comes when it's called. My peacocks do neither. They spread their tails with tremendous ceremony and there is no one there to see it half the time but a bewildered chicken or a delivery man who did not ask for the show and clearly wishes he could refuse the tip. They are indifferent to praise and worse than indifferent to correction. I have one old peafowl, I call him General Lee though he has done nothing to earn the rank but molt dramatically every summer as if shedding a uniform in surrender, who has taken to roosting on the hood of my car. He leaves it in a condition that suggests he has strong opinions about my driving.

They also have a way of looking at you sideways, out of that one flat eye, that makes you feel judged by something that ought by rights to know nothing of judgment, being a bird with a brain the size of a lima bean. I find this state of being looked down upon by my own poultry to be spiritually useful, in the way I suppose a hair shirt is useful, though a good deal noisier.

A puppy, now, would love me. It would follow me about and lick my hand and generally behave as though I had done something to deserve it, which we both know I have not. I don't believe I could stand the shock of being liked around here. Better to stick with the peacocks, who make their contempt plain and save me the trouble of wondering about it.

Give my regards to the puppy anyway, and tell it there are no hard feelings, only that I have already given my heart, for reasons no more sensible than most devotions, to a yard full of vain, screeching, ungrateful birds, and there does not seem to be room left over.

Yours,
Flannery
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short prose piece in epistolary form about a woman who keeps two dozen peafowl, explaining to a would-be dog-giver why dogs and peacocks don't mix, in a wry literary voice reminiscent of O'Connor's letters.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Mrs. Hutchins,

I received your letter offering me the pick of your setter's litter, and I want you to know I read it twice, once for the pleasure of it and once to make sure I would say no with proper gratitude.

You have been kind to think of me, but you have not thought of my peafowl, who would not survive the kindness. I keep twenty-four of them on this place, which is either a blessing or an affliction depending on the hour and whether they have roosted on the car again. They are vain, filthy, and glorious, and they do not share the ground with anything that pants.

I had a dog once. I will not tell you his name because it shames me to remember how highly I thought of him before the incident. He was a good dog, as dogs go, meaning he loved me indiscriminately and would have died for me without once wondering if I deserved it. He met my old peacock, the one I called Brother, in the yard on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday I had a dog with a torn ear and a peacock who screamed for four days as though the Last Judgment were arriving personally for him. Peafowl do not forgive. They do not even forget in the ordinary sense; they seem to consult the offense daily, like scripture.

You will tell me some dogs are gentle, and I believe you, the way I believe some snakes are harmless — I still do not care to find out which ones in my own yard. A peacock does not require an aggressive dog to come to ruin. He requires only a dog who is curious, and curiosity is the one vice no dog has ever been bred out of.

I have made my peace with a yard that is more theater than pasture. Every morning I am reminded that God, when He made the peacock, was not thinking about efficiency, or comfort, or the sensibilities of the neighbors, and I take that as instruction. I do not intend to introduce competing theology into the yard in the form of a setter pup, however sweet his disposition.

Give the pup to someone whose animals do not consider themselves persecuted royalty. I am, believe me, obliged to you, and will admire him from a distance, which is the only distance at which I admire anything with more enthusiasm than sense.

Yours in Christ and considerable feather dust,

Mary Elizabeth
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a playful, slightly eccentric letter response from a peacock breeder turning down a dog offer, with vivid descriptions of peacock antics and an invitation to visit the farm.
counterfactuals.output:
# From the Feathered Fields Peacock Farm

Dear Bartholomew,

What a curious proposition! A dog, you say — trained, loyal, and apparently possessed of "impeccable manners." I have no doubt Winston is a splendid creature, but I fear he would be terribly outnumbered here at Feathered Fields, where the true aristocracy struts on legs far spindlier than his own.

You see, I already have Sir Reginald, who spends his mornings admiring his reflection in the horse trough with the devotion of a man courting his own soul. He has fanned his tail at the mailman four times this week alone, each time with the unwavering confidence of a peacock who believes himself the reincarnation of a Renaissance prince. The mailman, I should note, has stopped ringing the bell and now simply lobs the parcels over the fence like a man fleeing a small, glittering dragon.

Then there's Josephine, who has taken to sleeping on the roof of the tool shed and shrieking at 5 a.m. with all the subtlety of a fire alarm wrapped in a feather boa. My neighbors have suggested therapy. I've suggested earplugs.

And don't get me started on the twins, Pomp and Circumstance, who spent last Tuesday in a magnificent standoff over a single unremarkable beetle, tails fully unfurled, strutting in slow circles like two opera divas refusing to share a stage.

A dog, however well-behaved, would only complicate this delicate ecosystem of vanity and volume. I imagine poor Winston attempting to herd them, only to be met with three hundred iridescent eyes blinking at him in collective, regal disdain.

So while I must regretfully decline your generous offer, I insist you come visit instead — bring Winston along, even, so long as he doesn't mind being upstaged. We'll have tea on the porch while Reginald performs his fifth reflection-inspection of the day, and I promise you'll leave with feathers in your hair and a story or two you won't quite believe yourself.

With great feathered affection,

**Eugenia P. Hawthorne**
*Keeper of Feathers, Mistress of Chaos*
Feathered Fields Peacock Farm
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
